HTS Code and Import Highlights by Component ........................................................................ 13 x This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. 1 Supply Chain for Large Power Transformers 1.1 Overview Large power transformers (LPTs) are critical infrastructure assets of the U.S. electric grid and hydropower fleet. They function primarily as generator step-up units and are typically rated at 100 MVA or greater (Office of Electricity Delivery and Energy Reliability 2014; Putsche et al. 2024) with high-side voltages2 of 100 kV (Office of Electricity Delivery and Energy Reliability 2014). LPTs are often custom designed and engineered to incorporate magnetic cores, copper or aluminum windings, insulating materials, and steel tanks, among other features. Their unit weights commonly range between 100 and 400 tons (Office of Electricity Delivery and Energy Reliability 2014), making them logistically challenging to transport and adding to their installed cost. Because multiple generating units may share a common transformer or a transformer bank, a single failure can curtail significant portions of plant output at once. For instance, at Chief Joseph Dam, failure of a single transformer bank has the potential to take numerous generating units offline simultaneously, amplifying both reliability and economic impacts. At Bonneville First Powerhouse, two units share a transformer bank, but their power transmission capability is deliberately restricted to reduce outage risks. These use cases highlight the vulnerability of shared configurations. Compounding this risk, replacement times for LPTs often exceed 18–36 months, making outages difficult to recover from and further emphasizing the importance of spares, monitoring, and coordinated replacement planning (Hydroelectric Design Center 2012). The U.S. LPT market is characterized by high demand, aging infrastructure, and limited domestic production capacity. The assembly landscape involves both centralized factory production and opportunities for on-site refurbishment in hydropower projects. Tank fabrication, integration of active parts, filling with insulating fluids, and rigorous testing are all precision- intensive steps requiring specialized infrastructure and highly skilled labor.
